---
title: "Predicting observations the model did not see"
---

A regression line may follow the reading times in our dataset very closely. But has the model learned a relation that will help us predict a response it has never seen, or has it learned peculiarities of these readers and stories? We cannot answer by looking at the same responses that were used to fit the line. We have to hide observations from the fitting procedure and see what happens when the model predicts them.

The phrase *hide observations* still leaves an important choice open. We might hide one response while retaining other responses from the same reader and story. We might instead hide every response from one reader, or every response from one story. These are three different prediction problems because the model has different information available in each case. We will call the full statement of what is hidden, what remains known, and how errors are averaged the **validation-target specification (VTS)**.

We will work with the corrected [Natural Stories data](https://github.com/languageMIT/naturalstories), which pair self-paced reading times with lexical and contextual predictors in ten construction-enriched stories ([Futrell et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-020-09503-7)). One row gives the button latency for one reader at one word position, along with the word's length, frequency, and surprisal. The [measurement discussion](prediction-targets.qmd#natural-stories-data) walks through a sentence and a response row before we define any split.

With the response in hand, we can specify the prediction target, separate training information from test information, and decide how to score an error. We then compare complete modeling procedures through [cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd), [likelihood-based criteria](information-criteria.qmd), [exact leave-one-out calculations](leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd), and posterior approximations such as [PSIS-LOO](psis-loo.qmd) and [WAIC](waic.qmd). At every stage, the question is the same: did the procedure predict information that was genuinely unavailable when it was fit?

```{r}
#| label: prediction-index-data

natural_all <- readRDS(
  "data/natural-stories/natural-stories-corrected.rds"
)
complete_prediction_row <- with(
  natural_all,
  is.finite(log_rt) & is.finite(word_length) &
    is.finite(log_unigram_frequency) & is.finite(gpt3_surprisal)
)
natural <- natural_all[complete_prediction_row, ]

prediction_inventory <- data.frame(
  object = c(
    "complete response rows",
    "participants",
    "stories",
    "sentences",
    "contextual word positions"
  ),
  count = c(
    nrow(natural),
    length(unique(natural$participant_id)),
    length(unique(natural$story_id)),
    length(unique(natural$sentence_id)),
    length(unique(paste(
      natural$story_id,
      natural$word_position,
      sep = ":"
    )))
  )
)

prediction_inventory
```

An [observed-minus-fitted residual](../regression-models/residuals.qmd) describes a response used to estimate a model. Its variance measures in-sample discrepancies around that fit; [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) here still means an expected squared deviation for a named random quantity. To learn how the complete procedure predicts an unavailable response, we must remove that response from fitting and define what *unavailable* means. In Natural Stories, it can mean one response row, every response from one participant, or every position in one story.

| predictive target | absent during fitting | still represented |
|:--|:--|:--|
| another response row | that latency | its participant and story |
| a new participant | every latency from that participant | the ten stories |
| an omitted enriched story | every latency from that story | the participant sample |

These targets are not interchangeable. A random row split cannot evaluate an absent participant or story because other rows from that group remain in training. Conversely, leave-one-story-out validation has only the released stories as transfer opportunities; the response-row count does not create that many independent text evaluations.

## Validation-target specification {#validation-target-specification}

We will call the five decisions that turn a split into a scientific claim the
**validation-target specification (VTS)**. Before fitting, state:

1. the **split unit** that moves as a block between training and test data;
2. the **score-aggregation unit** that receives equal weight in the reported loss;
3. the **prediction information set**, meaning what is known about a held-out unit;
4. the transformations, coefficients, and tuning decisions re-estimated inside each
   training fold; and
5. the population or collection to which the held-out result might transfer.

For instance, a participant-held-out Natural Stories analysis may split by reader,
average loss within readers before averaging readers, retain the lexical predictors
for each test word, refit standardization and regression coefficients in each fold,
and target similarly sampled readers of these ten stories. Changing any one entry
changes the claim. We refer to a disagreement between the declared entry and the
implemented computation as a **validation-target mismatch**.

## Defining and scoring a prediction

[Prediction targets](prediction-targets.qmd) state which responses or groups are new and which predictors remain available. [Training and test data](training-and-test-data.qmd) then enforce that separation, including training-only estimation of predictor transformations. A [predictive loss](predictive-loss.qmd) scores each held-out prediction. The [bias--variance tradeoff](bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd) explains why a procedure can closely fit one training sample yet vary across samples.

[Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd) rotates a row-level split. [Grouped cross-validation](grouped-cross-validation.qmd) instead moves complete participants or stories together. We keep the Natural Stories population regression fixed so that changing the split changes the predictive claim rather than the fitted predictor set. The model omits participant and story effects for this comparison. Reproducing the source paper's validation would require fitting its grouped structure anew inside every split.

## Comparing models

[Comparing predictive loss](comparing-predictive-loss.qmd) moves to MegaOrientation and evaluates additive and frame-specific ordinal models on verbs absent from fitting. This switch marks a conceptual break: the target becomes lexical transfer, and the response becomes ordered rather than continuous. The comparison thus follows the course's introduction to [cumulative logit regression](../regression-models/ordinal-regression.qmd). Its population fits omit participant and item heterogeneity, and the comparison remains conditional on the release's acceptability-selected predicate-frame inventory.

The final pages return to the Provo passage summaries used earlier in the course. [Likelihood-ratio tests](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd) compare nested Gaussian models; [information criteria](information-criteria.qmd) add fit penalties; [leave-one-out cross-validation](leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd), [PSIS-LOO](psis-loo.qmd), and [WAIC](waic.qmd) use matched observations and pointwise log-likelihood contributions. Each comparison keeps the response rows and candidate model family fixed.

Fix the prediction unit, split, and loss before comparing models. Otherwise a lower loss may answer a different prediction question. And even when two models answer the same question, successful prediction alone cannot identify a processing mechanism.

## Checking the module map

1. Can a random response-row split estimate performance for a reader whose responses
   are all absent during fitting?
2. If participants are held out but losses are pooled over rows, which unit receives
   equal weight?
3. Does lower held-out loss identify the cognitive mechanism that produced the
   responses?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. No. Other responses from that reader remain in the training set.
2. A response row receives equal weight; participants with more retained rows
   contribute more to the score.
3. No. Lower loss supports a predictive comparison for the declared VTS, while
   correlated predictors or alternative mechanisms may yield the same advantage.

</details>

## Recap and forward link

1. Name the prediction and validation units.
2. Keep every fitted decision inside the training data.
3. Compare compatible models using held-out loss or an explicitly stated
   approximation to that loss.

Begin with the [prediction target discussion](prediction-targets.qmd#natural-stories-data), which fixes the empirical object before any split is made.
